note: Genesis and Exodus are linked by this introduction (Gen. 46:8–27). God’s promise of nationhood to Abraham begins to be fulfilled by Israel’s fruitfulness (Gen. 12:2).

The number going into Egypt is sometimes given as seventy-five (Acts 7:14), with the difference due to who is counted. The Septuagint text adds five of Joseph’s further male descendants, yielding a total of seventy-five. See notes on Gen. 46:15–27.

The terms “fruitful,” “multiplied,” and “the land was filled” remind us of Gen. 1:26–28. Israel fulfills the mandate given to humankind in Gen. 1. By opposing the growth of the Israelites, Pharaoh sets himself against God’s purposes for humanity.

God’s multiplication of Israel leads to their oppression by the Egyptians.

**1:8a new king.** The beginning of a new era is marked off by the advent of a new pharaoh. This pharaoh may have been Ahmose I (1550–1525 B.C.) of the eighteenth dynasty, who expelled the Hyksos, the Semitic rulers of Egypt from about 1700–1550 B.C. (Introduction: Date and Occasion; Acts 7:18 note).

These cities for storing agricultural provisions and military supplies were located in the strategic Nile Delta region. Pithom was probably located at modern Tell er-Ratabah or at Tell Hisn, and Raamses is identified as modern Qantir. The city name Raamses was given to the location by Ramesses II (1279–1213 B.C.), who made the city his capital. Prior to this the city was known as Avaris during the period of the Hyksos, then possibly Peru-nefer before being renamed Raamses. Recent archaeological excavations at Qantir have revealed the remains of an impressive city from the second millennium, when a branch of the Nile flowed beside the city. When this branch silted up, Raamses was abandoned, with much of its valuable stonework being removed to Tanis.
The bitter oppression of Egypt is later commemorated by the bitter herbs of the Passover meal (12:8).

See note on Gen. 14:13.

**midwives.** Two midwives to serve such a large population seems far too few; they may be guild leaders. Their names are Semitic, and v. 15 identifies them as Hebrews. While the Pharaoh remains anonymous, the names of the two midwives live on.
This consisted of two stones upon which women in labor squatted.

A box of woven papyrus reeds, daubed with tar to make it watertight (cf. Job 9:26; Is. 18:2). The Hebrew term translated “basket” here is used for Noah’s craft in Gen. 7–9.
There is great irony in the fact that Pharaoh’s daughter rescues Moses from the Nile; her father had commanded the Egyptians to throw all male children into the river (1:22).

This name is Semitic (text note), though perhaps it is compatible with the Egyptian word _Mose_ meaning “born of” (e.g., _Thutmose,_ meaning “born of Thut”). He is educated in the Egyptian court as a promising young noble (Acts 7:22).

Now forty years old (Acts 7:23), Moses identifies himself with God’s people (Heb. 11:24–27). His effort to deliver an Israelite from oppression proves vain when he seeks to be a judge of Israel (v. 14). While the Israelite challenges Moses’s role as judge, God later appoints Moses to fulfill this task.

Probably the name of an early tribal confederacy operating in the Arabian desert. The Midianites were descendants of Abraham and Keturah (Gen. 25:1–6; Num. 10:29–32; Judg. 6).

An uncultivated area but capable of sustaining grazing livestock. According to 13:4 and Num. 10:11, the wilderness of Sinai later sustains Israel’s flocks for a year. Horeb and Sinai are terms that possibly distinguish Horeb as a wider region from Mount Sinai.

A real bush is illumined with supernatural fire. God is transcendent, but reveals Himself as fire in the bush to call Moses.
The spot is made sacred by God’s presence. See 19:23; 24:2. Only those who are holy can remain in God’s presence. Israel must become a holy nation if God is to dwell among them.

The inhabitants of the Syro-Palestinian coastland.

Probably Thutmose III (1479–1425 B.C.). See Introduction: Date and Occasion.
Moses felt inadequate for the task, as did Gideon (Judg. 6:15) and Jeremiah (Jer. 1:6). This is the first of his four objections (cf. v. 13; 4:1, 10).

God’s call will be confirmed by His future action. God will be with Moses to bring him back to worship (“serve God”) on this same mountain. Having served the Egyptians under duress, the Israelites will become God’s servants in response to His rescue of them.

Moses anticipates a question from the people regarding the identity of the God who has sent him back to Egypt. In Scripture, a personal name is not merely a form of address but a description of character and personality (Ps. 9:10; cf. 1 Sam. 25:25). In Genesis, God is known to the patriarchs by different names: e.g., God Most High; God Almighty; God Everlasting.

This expression, which builds on God’s promise to be with Moses (v. 12), repeats twice the word _ehyeh_ (“I AM”). God will be who He is. He does not change in His perfections. What He is now, He will be in the future. Other designations of God usually draw attention to some particular aspect of His nature. This expression is all-inclusive.

LORD **.** The Hebrew is _Yahweh,_ associated here by wordplay with the Hebrew verb for “to be” (thus meaning “he is” or “he will be”). The corresponding first person is _ehyeh,_ that is, “I am.” Note the parallels: “I AM has sent me” (v. 14) and “The Lord [Yahweh] ... has sent me” (v. 15).

**remembered throughout all generations.** Yahweh, the divine name particularly associated with God’s covenant relationship with Israel, is henceforth to be used in worship. English versions of the OT usually render the Hebrew name “Yahweh” as “the LORD.” The Jews thought the name too holy to pronounce, and when reading the text substituted _adonay_ (“my Lord”). The vowel signs for _adonay_ were later added to the Hebrew consonants of _Yahweh_ as a pronunciation reminder, and this hybrid form was rendered “Jehovah” by William Tyndale’s English translation (A.D. 1530).
These are family heads who represent Israel. They will be assembled to hear of God’s faithfulness (4:30, 31).
The usual biblical description of Canaan. The Hebrew term translated “honey” probably refers here to a sweet syrup derived from dates or grapes.
This mention of extraordinary deeds anticipates the miraculous events that will take place in Egypt (7:14–12:30).
As He promised, God will see that their years of bondage are recompensed (Gen. 15:14).

God gives Moses three miraculous signs to perform before the Israelites. Later, similar signs will be performed before the Pharaoh. Whereas the Israelites will believe, Pharaoh will disregard both these and subsequent signs warning of disaster.

**4:1 But behold.** Moses’s third objection (3:11 note). Israel must be persuaded. This will be a difficult task, but God has purposed to see that Israel will believe (3:18). Nothing is said here about convincing Pharaoh (cf. 6:12).

The Hebrew word for “hand” often connotes power. Against the oppressing hand of Egypt (3:8; 14:30; 18:10), the mighty hand of God will be stretched out (3:19–20). God will use the hand of Moses to show His power. Moses’s staff will become the staff of God (v. 20).
Not what is today called Hansen’s Disease, but a common skin disease of the time. God shows His power to judge and to heal.
The Nile was revered as a god and was the source of Egypt’s life.

The fourth objection. Moses claims not to be fluent, but God equips whom He calls (cf. Jer. 1:9). God is teaching Moses and his successors to depend on Him for their gifts. Since God made the mouth, He can enable a person to use it (v. 11).

Left without excuse, Moses still tries to decline his commission. But the Lord has already summoned his brother Aaron. The relation of Moses to Aaron sheds light on the nature of prophecy: Aaron will be a mouthpiece for Moses just as a prophet is for God (v. 16). See also 6:30; 7:1.
The supernatural events are again anticipated (3:20 note). These miraculous deeds will be performed with this same staff.
Including the Egyptian pharaoh (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

God will display His power over the stubborn hostility of the king so that His people might know that He is the Lord, their deliverer (6:6–8).

The Lord puts His claim upon Israel as His firstborn son. God’s claim is the reason for God’s deliverance and the covenant to be sealed at Sinai (“that he may serve me,” v. 23). This claim issues in God’s threat against Pharaoh’s firstborn (i.e., the firstborn of Egypt).

The Hebrew is slightly ambiguous. Most likely the attack is directed against Moses himself, perhaps because of his failure to circumcise his son. Alternatively, it may be against Moses’s firstborn, Gershom.

Presumably a ceremonial instrument. Zipporah intervenes to circumcise her son.

Aaron will now function as Moses’s spokesman (vv. 13–16 note).
Israel now believes as God said they would (3:18). They worship, praising God for His care.

The confrontation with Pharaoh begins with God’s demand. The people are His, not Pharaoh’s.

**hold a feast.** This is a pilgrimage to a shrine where a festival will be held (3:18).
LORD **?** Pharaoh’s question highlights an important theme within the book of Exodus. Subsequent events will make the Lord known.

After presenting God’s demand, Moses and Aaron seek to reason with Pharaoh. The Lord is the God of the Hebrews; the distance will be only a three-day journey (3:18); and Israel’s disobedience to God’s command might seriously reduce Pharaoh’s work force.
Later this term comes to mean the responsible landowners in Israel (2 Kin. 11:18–20; Jer. 34:19), but here it means peasant workers attached to the land.
The bricks of the time were much larger than modern bricks; they were molded of Nile mud with straw to increase their strength.

**were urgent.** The taskmasters continue to pressure the people to produce the same number of bricks as before.

LORD **... judge.** Not for the last time, the leaders of Israel curse Moses for obeying the command of the Lord.

As a mediator, Moses speaks God’s Word to the people, and he pleads the plight of the people to God. This pattern is repeated throughout Exodus. God’s reply gives assurance that the hopeless situation will be the occasion for His mighty action (see ch. 6).
The Lord’s power will more than prevail. Pharaoh will not only let them go, he will _drive_ Israel out.

Note the repeated use of the revelation (authority) formula, “I am the LORD,” in these verses (vv. 2, 6–8). The use of God’s name underscores the surety of His covenant promises and faithfulness (3:15 and notes).

God had revealed Himself to the patriarchs as God Almighty (Hebrew _El Shaddai_; cf. Gen. 17:1; 28:3; 35:11). Throughout Genesis, however, the name _Yahweh_ is much more commonly used, and it was clearly known by the patriarchs (e.g., Gen. 15:7). While some scholars suggest that the significance of the name _Yahweh_ was not fully known by the patriarchs, it is more likely that the final part of v. 3 ought to be translated: “My name is _Yahweh_. Did I not make myself known to them?”
Yahweh is also El Shaddai, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. His covenant promises to these earlier patriarchs include the gift of the land of Canaan.
When used of God, “remembered” means that He is prepared to act on His promises, not simply recall them.

God’s reply to Moses’s complaint of 5:22–23. This is the central core of the section, a solemn assurance of redemption and of covenant reaffirmation. The concept of redemption points to the redemptive work of Christ for His people (Luke 4:16–21; Gal. 3:13; 4:5; Heb. 9:15).

**redeem.** This term normally refers to the restoration of rights to a disadvantaged family member by the payment of a price or a ransom; such redemption was normally effected by the next of kin (Lev. 25:25; cf. Ruth 4). Israel, as Yahweh’s son (4:22), is redeemed from Egypt to be God’s own people. Redemption and covenant relation are the keys to the passage. The heart of the covenant is God’s claim on His people and the reciprocal claim that He allows them to make on Him.
This anticipates 19:5–6.
In spite of God’s renewed promise, the Israelites remain unconvinced, and even Moses has difficulty believing that his mission will be effective.

The genealogical material in vv.14–25 interrupts the flow of the story, which is picked up in vv. 26–30; these latter verses deliberately echo vv. 10–12. In this transitional section, Moses and Aaron are formally identified, and the story of their work is reviewed and resumed in preparation for the description of the signs and wonders. The formal identification is accomplished through a genealogy that begins with Reuben, Israel’s oldest son, then proceeds to Simeon, the second son, and finally to Levi. Levi’s genealogy establishes the link to Moses and Aaron. Among the Levites Amram is singled out, then Aaron and Moses. The subsequent names constitute the priestly line for Israel (Num. 25:10–13; 26:57–62). For Korah, see Num. 16:1–35.

The record of the marriage of Amram to his paternal aunt would be most unlikely if the genealogy were fictional. Such a marriage was later forbidden in the Mosaic Law (Lev. 18:12), so an author who was making up the genealogy to put Moses’s family in the best light possible would certainly not have invented such a potentially scandalous relationship. The form of the genealogy changes between vv. 19 and 20, suggesting that the Amram of v. 20 was a different person than the Amram of v. 18. The genealogy deliberately omits a number of generations while still establishing that Aaron and Moses were descended from Levi. Three women are mentioned in tracing the line: Jochebed, Elisheba, and a daughter of Putiel.

No descendant of Moses is named, but those of Aaron continue for the next two generations to establish priestly succession from Aaron through his successor Eleazar. The genealogy spans only four generations for the sojourn in Egypt and is clearly selective (Gen. 5:3–32 note).
Those named appear later in the story of Israel’s time in the wilderness.
Having told Moses what he should say to the Israelites (6:6–8), the Lord now instructs him regarding Pharaoh. His real demand now appears: not a temporary absence, but a definitive exodus from Egypt.
The function of Aaron in relation to Moses demonstrates the function of a true prophet in relation to God (4:13–16 note).

These verses provide an insight into God’s purpose in sending a series of supernatural events against the Egyptians. As v. 5 highlights, these events are designed to make God known to the Egyptians, addressing Pharaoh’s earlier question, “Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go?” (5:2). In order to fulfill this aim, God states that He will “harden Pharaoh’s heart.” This is a difficult concept to grasp, complicated by the fact that whereas in English the idiom “to be hard-hearted” implies that one lacks compassion, in Hebrew it implies that one is determined or resolved to do something, not necessarily with negative connotations. At no point does God cause Pharaoh to act contrary to his own desires. On the contrary, He actually gives Pharaoh the courage to remain stubbornly committed to his initial plan. Remarkably, God does not use force to manipulate other people to do His will. Pharaoh is allowed to resist—even when the signs and wonders clearly indicate that such resistance will ultimately be futile.

The Hebrew is a broad term describing the center of feeling, thinking, and willing.

**though I multiply.** Or, “in order that I might multiply.”

**my signs and wonders.** The expression “signs and wonders” is the one used most regularly in the rest of the OT to denote the events that took place in Egypt (cf. Deut. 4:34; 6:22; 7:19; 26:8; 29:3; 34:11; Neh. 9:10; Pss. 105:27; 135:9; Jer. 32:20). Although it has become customary to speak of these as the “ten plagues,” this designation is misleading. Whereas today the term “plague” is generally understood to denote some form of infectious disease, it previously meant in English a “blow” or “stroke” (based on the Latin term _plaga_). In the Hebrew text of Exodus, the signs and wonders are presented as a series of blows that God sends against the Egyptians, blows often symbolized by the use that Aaron and Moses make of the “staff of God” (4:20).

verse_quote: shall know ... bring out the people.
note: God’s purpose in saving the Israelites from Egypt is not merely for their good but so that people will know that He is the Lord (cf. 18:10–12; see Introduction: Theology of Exodus).

The Hebrew word here (different from the word for “serpent” in 4:3) often refers to a reptile associated with water (Gen. 1:21; Ezek. 29:3; 32:2). A crocodile may be in view. Alternatively, it might be a cobra, which is a major symbol for the land of Egypt.
The Hebrew term refers to priests who were associated with the worship of Egyptian deities. Their power to perform miracles may be occultic. See note on 9:11.
LORD **had said.** As predicted in 4:21 (cf. 7:3).

A theory of natural causes for the signs and wonders does not do justice to the clear statements of the text (7:17; 9:5 notes). A particular order would be essential for an explanation of the plagues as normal events associated with the overflow of the Nile, but neither the narrative here, nor the lists in Ps. 78:44–51; 105:28–36, suggest such an order.

The signs and wonders are arranged in three groups of three (7:14–8:19; 8:20–9:12; 9:13–10:29), preceded by the transformation of Moses’s staff into a reptile (7:9–13) and climaxed by the death of the firstborn (12:29–32). In the first plague of each series, Moses contacts Pharaoh in the morning; no time indication is given for the other two. The first two plagues in each sequence are preceded by a divine warning, but the third comes unheralded. There is a progression in the severity of the signs, as gradually God persuades some of the Egyptians to take seriously Moses’s request for the release of the Israelites. Pharaoh, however, remains resistant to letting them go.

**7:14 hardened.** Pharaoh’s heart is strong; he possibly takes courage from the fact that his sorcerer-priests are able to duplicate what Moses and Aaron did.

Repeated references to the rod point to Yahweh as the source of power for all that occurs.

**I will strike.** Aaron will strike, but the Lord will perform the miracle (vv. 14– 20). The striking is by God’s hand, by His rod. The deed of Aaron is owned by God no less than the word that God gave him through Moses.

**blood.** In Hebrew the word never denotes its red color, but always blood as a substance. The red clay that comes down at the time of flooding from the Ethiopian highlands (coloring the Nile water red) is not in view.

All the natural waters of Egypt are involved, including the natural arms of the Nile, the irrigation canals, and the pools formed by river flooding. The Nile River, the source of Egypt’s agricultural life, was revered as a god by the Egyptians in Moses’s day. Beginning with this plague, the Lord’s superiority over the Egyptian pantheon of gods is demonstrated.
See note on 7:11.
Here the allegedly divine river and frogs bring misery on the Egyptians—another demonstration of the Lord’s supremacy.
The sorcerer-priests can only add to the distress (9:11 note).

verse_quote: I will let the people go.
note: Pharaoh, personally affected, makes his first concession. However, he will renege on his promise once the frogs are removed.
God raises His rod against the dust, turning it into an outbreak of gnats or, perhaps more likely, lice.
The magicians now admit that a divine intervention is directly involved (cf. 31:18; Ps. 8:3), but Pharaoh is not persuaded.
This first plague of the second sequence again finds Pharaoh at the Nile (cf. 7:15).
See text note. In the second set of the three signs, God distinguishes between Goshen and the rest of Egypt. He shows His favor toward His own people. Pharaoh later investigates this (9:7).

During the swarms of flies, Pharaoh offers to let the people sacrifice, but he is not prepared to agree to all that the Lord demands. Moses regularly refuses to compromise: he will neither worship in the land nor go less than a three-day journey (v. 28); neither will he leave behind the women and children (10:9–11) nor the flocks and herds (10:24–26). At last, after Pharaoh repeatedly breaks faith, God’s liberation is total. Israel not only goes out to worship at Sinai but leaves Egypt for Canaan.
The ancient Egyptians may have deified the animals customarily sacrificed by the Israelites, but some other reason, now unknown, may have caused the Egyptians to abhor Israelite sacrifices.

The horse was brought into Egypt by the Hyksos (c. 1700 B.C.).

**camels.** Though sporadically used during this period (cf. Gen. 12:16), widespread use of the camel in Egypt only came much later. Perhaps camels of the merchant traders from Arabia and elsewhere are referred to here.
The wonder has not come by coincidence. The biblical account gives no room for a naturalistic explanation.
Since the next plague affects livestock also, this phrase must designate either “all kinds of livestock” or all the livestock in the field (cf. vv. 18–19).
See 8:23 and note.
This is done before Pharaoh to underscore that the event is supernatural.

The defeat of the sorcerer-priests has been clear from the start, when Aaron’s staff-become-reptile swallowed up the reptiles they produced (7:12). They have been able to imitate turning water to blood and producing frogs, but they have been able only to add to, and not reverse, these wonders (7:22; 8:7). When they cannot imitate the production of lice (or gnats), they tell Pharaoh that this is of divine origin (8:18, 19). Finally, the magicians are struck with boils and retreat in discomfort and disgrace (9:11).

These plagues (lit. “blows” or “strokes”) show the power of God’s hand in striking Egypt (3:20; 7:25; 12:13). The last three wonders fall when the staff of the Lord is stretched out to heaven, earth, and heaven (9:22; 10:13, 21). Ex. 9:13–19 is one of the longest speeches in the plagues cycle, with God explaining His own actions.

God’s actions are tempered by mercy. He withholds total destruction so that the Egyptians might know His power and repent (v. 15). Further, God’s actions against Pharaoh will cause God’s name to be proclaimed to the nations., 16
Some Egyptians learn to fear God’s word (10:7)., 21

Pharaoh confesses his guilt for the first time, but the phrase “this time” points to the superficiality of his confession. Though not believing him, Moses nevertheless shows God’s power over the earth by stopping the hail.

note: This information seems to set the time in January–February, a time when hailstorms are frequent in Egypt. Flax was in the bud in January. Barley was in the ear at that time; it would have been harvested in February., 32
Pharaoh’s will is strengthened four times in this one narrative: vv. 8, 10–11, 16–17, 20.
A clear statement of the divine plan involving Pharaoh. The signs and wonders are designed to teach Israel and to leave an indelible impression on their posterity (Deut. 6:20–25).
Moses demands that Israel’s permission to worship be unqualified and total. See note on 8:25.
Pharaoh is willing to let the men go, but not the rest of the Israelite population. Note the sarcasm of v. 10.
Goshen is presumably exempt.
The speed of Pharaoh’s action and his confession of sin underscore Egypt’s peril. Severe famine is threatened (“Not a green thing remained”; see v. 15).

This darkness is clearly more than a blinding sandstorm or an eclipse of the sun. It is an unnatural darkness, like that associated with the day of the Lord (Is. 8:22; 58:10; Joel 2:2; Amos 5:20; Zeph. 1:15; cf. Deut. 28:29). This supernatural darkness is further demonstration of the Lord’s authority and power over nature and the false gods of Egypt. The ancient Egyptians regarded Amon-Ra, the personification of the sun, as their chief deity. In this plague, he is not allowed to shine and give life to his people.

A different Hebrew word for “plague” (9:14 note) is used to emphasize the climactic act of divine judgment—the death of the firstborn. The Hebrew word means “stroke” or “blow” and was translated into Latin by the term _plaga_, from which comes the English term “plague.” Unfortunately, the term “plague” today is generally understood to be a synonym for “pestilence” rather than meaning a strike or blow, which is what it meant when the KJV was translated.
All four references to this event (3:21–22; 11:2–3; 12:35–36; Ps. 105:36–38) emphasize that Egypt gives gladly because of the Lord’s intervention.
The grinding of corn was menial work done by slaves and prisoners of war.

The first month of the Hebrew year was Abib (March–April). This verse appears to report the institution of this new religious calendar, in commemoration of the exodus. In the later Babylonian calendar, the month of Abib is called Nisan (Neh. 2:1; Esth. 3:7).

Like the sacrifices of Israel (e.g., Lev. 1:3), the Passover lamb must be without flaw. The idea of substitution is evident—the lamb dies in place of the firstborn. Jesus, whose death is prefigured by the Passover sacrifice, is called “the Lamb of God” and “the firstborn” (John 1:29, 36; Rom. 8:29; Col. 1:15, 18; 1 Pet. 1:19; Heb. 1:6; Rev. 5:6).
The slaughter occurs at sunset (Deut. 16:6). The act marks the beginning of the Passover.
Blood symbolizes the life of a victim (Lev. 17:11).
The Passover meal must be eaten as if in haste—the lamb roasted whole and accompanied by unleavened bread. The bitter herbs recall the bitter suffering of slavery in Egypt (1:14)., 9

The story has arrived at a climactic moment, and the Hebrews must be ready to flee immediately. Their garments, which resemble loose skirts, must be tied up in preparation for a hasty departure.

**Passover.** The Passover observance is the oldest of the Jewish festivals and is celebrated at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month (12:6). It is described in many key OT texts in addition to ch. 12 (cf. 34:25; Lev. 23:5–8; Num. 9:1–14; 28:16–25; 2 Chr. 30:1–9). It is immediately followed by the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which runs for the next seven days (the fifteenth through the twenty-first). Due to the hasty departure of the Israelites from Egypt, only the Passover is observed on this inaugural occasion. Later participants are garbed for travel to celebrate the exit of Israel from Egypt in haste and anxiety. The practice of ritual questions posed by the children during the Passover celebration is a later development rooted in vv. 26, 27.

The NT establishes a direct redemptive connection between the Passover and the death of Jesus, the supreme Passover Lamb who was sacrificed for those who believe (1 Cor. 5:7).

verse_quote: on all the gods of Egypt ... judgments.
note: The impotence of Egypt’s deities to protect the land’s inhabitants is vividly demonstrated to all.
Due to the haste of their departure from Egypt, the Israelites are unable to bake bread leavened with yeast. Unleavened bread becomes a symbol of their swift departure.

verse_quote: cut off from the congregation of Israel.
note: See note on Lev. 7:20. Resident aliens and native-born non-Israelites were expected to observe this regulation.

Hyssop was a species of marjoram used for purification (Lev. 14:4–6; Num. 19:6, 18; Ps. 51:7). The richly textured branches and leaves held enough blood to perform the required act. Hyssop has many stalks, and its use prevents the blood of the animal from coagulating.
The precise identity of the “destroyer” is uncertain; the alternative translation “destruction” may be preferable.
See “The Sacraments” at Matt. 28:19.
See note on v. 11. In Jewish Passover celebrations today, the youngest child asks the ritual question, and the father then recites the story of the exodus (cf. 13:8).
The threefold command underscores Pharaoh’s urgency. He admits defeat.
The blessing sought is presumably to countermand the dreadful curse that has gone through the land.
These actions confirm the statement in 11:3 (cf. 3:22).

See note 1:11. Succoth cannot be precisely located but must have been in the eastern Delta, possibly at Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat. The coastal routes to Canaan (13:17) were shorter but well guarded.

**six hundred thousand men on foot.** Males of military age (v. 41 note; cf. Num. 11:21; 26:51). Against objections that this number is too large, it has been argued that four centuries might well produce such numbers (1:7). As is often suggested, the Hebrew word for “thousand” can also be taken as meaning “family” or some subsection of a tribe such as a clan (Judg. 6:15). Others have argued that certain numbers were inadvertently altered on account of scribal misreading, which may explain the differences evident between other portions of the biblical text as presently known (cf. 2 Sam. 10:18 and 1 Chr. 19:18; See Introduction to Numbers: Special Issues).

Perhaps persecuted minorities or other slaves come with them. Egyptians who had intermarried with the Hebrews, and even God-fearing Egyptians, are doubtless also included (cf. 9:19–20; 12:48; Is. 56:3).
See Gen. 15:13; note on Acts 7:6.
The Hebrew term denotes clans (cf. 6:19).

This added explanation of the Passover regulations, focusing on the restriction of the ceremony to the covenant community, is occasioned by the mention of non-Israelites leaving Egypt with Israel (v. 38). Only circumcised covenant members are eligible to participate.

None of the meat is to be taken outside of the house where non-covenant members can have access to it.

**bones.** No bones of the animals are to be broken, perhaps as a symbol of covenant unity. As with the Passover lamb, no bones of Jesus were broken at His crucifixion (John 19:36; cf. 1 Cor. 5:7).

Due to the Passover, firstborn males of humans and cattle belong to the Lord (cf. vv. 11–16). The firstborn from the womb represents God’s claim on all. The principle is enunciated here and the details are given at 13:12–16; 22:29, 30; 34:19, 20. In this way, Jesus is later presented as Mary’s firstborn (Luke 2:22–23).
See note on 12:26.

Interpreting this figurative expression literally, Jews later put brief passages of the Law (13:1–10, 11–16; Deut. 6:4–9; 11:13–21) in small boxes and attached them to the left arm and forehead. These are the _tephillim,_ the phylacteries (protections) of later Judaism, to which Jesus refers in criticizing the Pharisees’ ostentatious displays of piety (Matt. 23:5).

An animal from the herd or flock can be given to the Lord as a whole burnt offering. The firstborn son is always to be redeemed (v. 13).

**firstborn ... males.** See note on v. 2.
This does not involve the shedding of blood and is not a sacrifice.
Like the Passover ritual (12:26, 27; 13:8), the ransom of the firstborn is to remind the Israelites that their firstborn males had been ransomed from death.

Israel is not exempted from the death sentence on the firstborn in Egypt. The firstborn were spared only through the blood of the Passover lamb. Subsequent generations must be ransomed, either through the life consecration of the Levites, chosen by God in place of the firstborn (Num. 3:11–13), or through the redemption price of five shekels (Num. 3:46–51).

The strongly fortified caravan route that ran parallel to the Mediterranean coast (see Introduction: Special Issues). The Philistines were not in Palestine in considerable numbers until the twelfth century B.C., but there may have been coastal pockets of Philistine (Minoan) trading colonies there earlier.

The Hebrew term (_yam suph_) is used to designate the Gulf of Aqaba (23:31), the Gulf of Suez (10:19; Num. 33:10), as well as the body of water crossed in the Exodus. Scholars suggest that the term may mean “sea of reeds” or “sea of the end.” The “Red Sea” of the exodus was probably one of the Bitter Lakes north of the Gulf of Suez. Perhaps it was the southern extension of the present Lake Menzaleh, or possibly it was Lake Ballah. Archaeological evidence suggests that the Bitter Lakes were at one time joined to the Gulf of Suez.

**equipped for battle.** This expression translates a rare Hebrew word that may not necessarily have military connotations. “In an orderly fashion” might be a better translation, especially given what is said in v. 17.
Moses fulfills the request made by Joseph centuries earlier (cf. Gen. 50:25; Josh. 24:32).
Israel camps on the edge of the wilderness near what may have been an Egyptian fortress at Etham (since the name seems Egyptian), where they understandably turn back (14:2).
Customary symbols of the immediate presence of God (3:2 note; 33:9–10; 40:34–38; Num. 9:15–22; 11:25; Pss. 99:7; 105:39). God guides Israel day and night by His presence.

By divine command, Israel turns back and camps at Pi-hahiroth. This invites Pharaoh’s pursuit (cf. vv. 3–4).

**Migdol.** A general word for “fortification”; its location is presently unknown.

**Baal-zephon.** This site (“Baal of the North”) may have been a shrine dedicated to the worship of a god who was viewed as a protector of sailors. The precise location of Baal-zephon is unknown.

Pharaoh is in earnest since his elite chariot force is deployed. The horse and chariot seem to have been introduced into Egypt by the Hyksos (c. 1700 B.C.). The Egyptian chariot normally carried two men, although it may have been accompanied by another man who was a runner.
Israel’s rebellious complaints against God’s leading are a continuing theme in Exodus (5:21; 15:24; 16:3; 17:2; 32:1).

At the crucial point of Israel’s deliverance they must see that their salvation is entirely God’s work. His signs and wonders in Egypt, His leading Israel to this hopeless impasse, pinned between Pharaoh’s chariots and the sea—all prepare for the climactic display of His saving power. The Lord will fight for them; they need only be still. He will gain the glory (14:18).

LORD **will fight.** This phrase indicates the origin of the theme of the Lord as “divine Warrior,” celebrated in ch. 15. War in the ancient world was viewed as a sacred undertaking in which the honor of the deity was at stake. In Israel, God was the “God of the armies of Israel” (1 Sam. 17:45), but also the “Lord of Hosts” (i.e., the Lord of the armies of heaven, the architect of Israel’s victories and the inflicter of Israel’s defeats). An early account of Israel’s conquests under the Lord’s leadership was called “the Book of the Wars of the Lord” (Num. 21:14). The theology of Holy War, which arose as a result, finds expression throughout both the OT and NT.
A prayer of Moses is to be understood.
The rod of Moses, used in bringing God’s signs and wonders on Egypt, will now bring salvation to His people.
The Angel of the Lord is identified with God’s own presence in the cloud (23:20–22). See note on Gen. 16:7.
God sends the wind to accomplish His purpose.

The night was divided into three watches of four hours, the last of which (the morning watch) was from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m., often the time for surprise attacks (cf. 1 Sam. 11:11). The Lord Himself throws the Egyptian army into confusion.
LORD **fights.** Egypt recognizes the victory as God’s (cf. v. 14).
The outstretched hand and staff of Moses are the instruments of destruction for the pursuing army, and they bring about Israel’s deliverance.
LORD **saved Israel.** Verses 30, 31 summarize God’s saving deed and its effect on Israel.

LORD **and in his servant Moses.** At this point, Israel is a community that professes faith. Later, in the wilderness, they will apostatize and come under God’s wrath (Num. 14; Ps. 95). The church, as a professing community, must avoid this example (1 Cor. 10:6–12).

Moses and Israel sing of deliverance and hope. The poem of vv. 1–18, unique in the OT, is a victory song expressed in the first person singular, sung by Moses and all the people. It celebrates the Lord’s majestic power in saving Israel at the sea (vv. 1–13) and claims His power in planting Israel in the land (vv. 14–18). The song’s many archaic expressions point to its origin in the Mosaic period.

**15:1 I will sing.** The Lord has shown His glory as He promised, and it is the privilege of His people to praise the God of their salvation. The form of the Hebrew verb indicates that this song was sung regularly by the Israelites thereafter.
The theme of Yahweh as the Divine Warrior is emphasized. See Is. 59:16–18.

A symbol of power. In Canaanite art the god Baal was sometimes depicted with a mace upheld in his right hand. Here, the symbol of divine power is the outstretched hand of Moses holding the rod of the Lord.

Through the threatening waters of death God brings His people to Himself. The waters are an instrument of judgment for Egypt and a means of deliverance for Israel. Paul, with some support from Jewish tradition, understands the Red Sea crossing as Israel’s “baptism” (1 Cor. 10:2; cf. 1 Pet. 3:21 note).
The staccato repetition of these first person claims reveals an arrogance that is soon silenced.
The comparison is rhetorical in this threefold presentation of God’s nature and power.
An expression for their reception into the abode of the dead (Pss. 63:9; 71:20).

This translates the Hebrew word _hesed,_ the precise sense of which is difficult to render in English. Here it refers to God’s loyalty and devotion to His people, a loyalty created by the bond of God’s covenant with them. Though we might expect it to be used for the devotion of God’s people to Him, its overwhelming use in the OT is as a description of God’s devotion to His people. There is no stronger term to express the free and faithful grace of His love (34:6, “abounding in steadfast love”; Ps. 136, “his steadfast love endures forever”). God’s abiding covenant love and mercy find particular illustration in the book of Hosea (Hos. 2:19).

**your holy abode.** The term used here denotes a temporary resting place, which shepherds might use. While Sinai represents the Lord’s resting place at this moment in the exodus, Zion ultimately serves as the place where God gathers His people and dwells among them.

The extraordinary, divinely induced fear of the inhabitants of Canaan is here depicted (Deut. 2:25 note). The peoples are mentioned in the approximate order they will be encountered by the Israelites as they journey to the Promised Land.

An important summary of the aims of the exodus that gives prominence to the motif of God dwelling on the earth. The purpose is the settlement of Israel as God’s special people in the Promised Land, the sanctuary of God’s dwelling.

**your own mountain.** The point of contact between heaven and earth will be here. The OT regularly associates God’s earthly dwelling place with mountains. Here the whole of Palestine is viewed as the place of revelation (cf. Ps. 78:54; Is. 11:9).

**sanctuary.** The land will become such by God’s indwelling presence, reminding readers that the goal of the exodus is the worship of God in the land. Apart from God’s gracious presence, there is no point in going to the land (33:15).

LORD **will reign.** Apart from two other explicit references to God’s kingship in the Pentateuch (Num. 23:21; Deut. 33:5), the tabernacle is presented as a royal tent. The concept of divine covenant with Israel involved a recognition of God’s kingship (1 Sam. 8:6–9).

As the Lord leads His people into the wilderness, He tests and delivers them in ways that reveal His purposes. He heals bitter water to show Himself as the Healer (15:22–27); gives manna and quail to show Himself as Provider and the one who establishes rest (Sabbath) for His people (16:1–26); and gives the water of life (17:1–7). Finally, in military victory, it is the Lord Himself who is the ensign of His people (17:15).

**15:22 wilderness of Shur.** Israel travels in the Sinai peninsula (about 260 miles [418 km] long and 150 miles [240 km] wide). The word “wilderness” refers here to grazing land as opposed to cultivated land. Shur was located northeast of the Sinai Peninsula, between Egypt and Palestine (Gen. 16:7; 20:1; 25:18).

The word means “bitterness.” The location is suggested to be modern Ain Hawarah, inland and 50 miles (80 km) south of the northern end of Suez. Apparently Israel went down the west coast of the peninsula until they turned east toward Sinai.

The first instance of Israel’s wilderness complaint—behavior that typifies Israel’s unbelief in the wilderness. The situation is critical. After nine days the water skins are empty, and death from dehydration is an immediate threat. Further, their hopes are dashed—they have located water, but have found it undrinkable (v. 23).

The complaint of the people directed to Moses is really against God. Since Moses leads at God’s command (17:1), he appeals to the Lord.

**showed.** God instructs Moses by showing him a tree. The general term for God’s law (Hebrew _torah_) is a form of the verb “showed.” God’s revelation in this event is a “statute and a rule,” preparing for the statutes and ordinances to be given at Sinai and then inscripturated as God’s Word written. God’s Word instructs Israel as He leads and tests them (cf. Jesus’ use of Deut. 8:3 in Matt. 4:4). The tree is a sign of healing and sweetness (Gen. 2:9; Judg. 9:11; Jer. 8:22; Ezek. 47:7, 8).

See Deut. 28:26, 60–62; 7:15. Diseases mark the effects of the divine curse.

**I am the** LORD **, your healer.** God has the power and the mercy to heal (Deut. 32:39; Ps. 103:3). He alone can heal in the peace of His salvation (2 Chr. 16:12; Is. 38:17). To the prayer of anguish (Jer. 17:14), God responds (Jer. 30:17; 33:6). Healing from the damage inflicted by sin and death will come through the Lord’s Anointed, by whose wounds we are healed (Is. 53:5; 61:1,2; Matt. 8:17).

The precise location of this site is uncertain. The Lord, who healed the water of Marah (v. 23), leads His people to a place of rest and refreshment. Had the people trusted God fully, there would have been no need to grumble at Marah. Elim was only a short distance away.

The Israelites continue their journey toward Mt Sinai. A theophany occurs in response to the people’s complaints (16:9–13). The chapter draws to a close with a rest on the following Sabbath (16:27–30). Israel’s keeping of the Sabbath prior to the revelation at Sinai is highlighted, as is God’s continued testing of Israel (v. 4; cf. 15:25; 17:2).

**16:1 wilderness of Sin.** Situated in the southwest of Sinai.

The people cry for bread and meat (v. 3), and God will give both (v. 8). Manna is called the “bread of the angels” (Ps. 78:25). In John 6:26–58, Jesus calls Himself the true manna (“bread of life”) of which this provision in the wilderness was a symbol and type.
The word normally refers to the manifested presence of God. Here, the Lord’s gracious provision of the manna is in view.

These small migratory game birds of the partridge family come from their winter habitat in Africa in the spring. They are miraculously provided by God to demonstrate His concern for the hunger of the Israelites (see Ps. 78:27). The gift of quail prepares for the sending of manna, which will become the daily food of the Israelites. Quail are given only on one other occasion (Num. 11).

An elevated term normally reserved for holy festivals. The implication is that the weekly Sabbath was normally kept by Israel before Sinai. The Sabbath ordinance in the Ten Commandments represents a codification of Sabbath observance, not its inauguration.
This seed is small, globular, grayish, and aromatic, tasting like honey cakes.
To commemorate the gift of manna, a daily portion is preserved in a special container, called “the golden urn” in Heb. 9:4. Normally, any manna kept overnight decomposed rapidly and became inedible.
The manna continues until they come to Canaan (Josh. 5:10–12). The nomadic lifestyle of the Israelites in the wilderness prevents them from growing crops.
This region, generally identified with the modern Wadi Refayid, about eight miles (13 km) south of Jebel Musa, is the last stop before Sinai.

This translates the Hebrew word _rib,_ which appears in the name “Meribah” (v. 7).

**test the** LORD **.** It is not Moses who is being put on trial, but God. God is being accused of abandoning Israel to die of thirst in the desert. Previously, God indicated that He would test the Israelites through their wilderness experience.
Moses, taking his rod in his hand and accompanied by elders of Israel who are summoned as representative witnesses of the nation, is to pass on before the people (cf. v. 6).

God stands on or beside the rock and is identified with it. God is called the “Rock” in the song of Moses (Deut. 32:4, 15, 18, 31) and in the psalms that speak of this event (Ps. 78:35; 95:1).

**strike the rock.** Moses lifts the rod associated with God’s power and strikes the rock. The fearful solemnity of Moses’s blow appears when he later strikes the rock in disobedience, thereby dishonoring the holiness of God (Num. 20:9–12).
Only here and in Ps. 95:8 are Meribah and Massah used in combination with reference to these events. The shorter name Massah is used in place of Massah and Meribah in Deut. 6:16; 9:22; 33:8.

The Amalekites, a nomadic group based in southern Palestine, were possibly descendants of Esau (Gen. 36:12–16). The Amalekites attacked from the rear (Deut. 25:18). God has provided manna from heaven and water from the rock; now He provides deliverance from enemies.

Joshua, an Ephraimite previously known as Hoshea (“salvation”), is called Joshua (“Yahweh saves”) at Kadesh, possibly as a result of this victory (Num. 13:8, 16).

**I will stand ... with the staff.** Joshua will choose men to fight, but they will do so under the uplifted staff, the sign of the Lord’s victory.

Joshua prevails in this battle only when Moses holds up to heaven the staff symbolizing the Lord’s presence that brought the signs and wonders in Egypt (4:2; 9:23) and dried up the sea (14:16).

**Hur.** Hur, attested in later tradition as the husband of Moses’s sister Miriam, was possibly the grandfather of the famous artisan of the tabernacle, Bezalel (1 Chr. 2:19–20).
One of several references to writing in Exodus. The account was perhaps written in the Book of the Wars of the Lord that is mentioned in Num. 21:14.

LORD **Is My Banner.** The Hebrew word translated “banner” underlies “staff” in v. 9 and is used for the “pole” on which the bronze serpent will later be placed (Num. 21:8). Since “banner” suggests cloth to us, this connection is lost. A spear could serve as a standard in battle, with or without bits of cloth tied to it. Moses’s staff is the ensign to which Joshua’s army can look and that symbolizes God’s saving power. Moses declares that God Himself is the standard, the ensign of His people.

LORD **.** The Hebrew is difficult to translate and interpret (cf. text note). The central message is nevertheless clear: God gives Israel the victory, and the continuing warfare between Israel and Amalek is the Lord’s. On the historic enmity between Israel and Amalek, see Num. 24:20; Deut. 25:17; 1 Sam. 15:2–33; 27:8, 9; 30:1–20; 2 Sam. 8:11, 12; 1 Chr. 4:42, 43; Esth. 3:1 note.

The visit of Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’s father-in-law, provides an important hinge in the book of Exodus, linking what has already occurred with the covenant about to be ratified. The first half of ch. 18 records Jethro’s reaction to the report of all that God has done for the Israelites in releasing them from Pharaoh’s control. Jethro responds appropriately by worshipping God. The second half of ch. 18 anticipates how the covenant will impact the daily lives of the Israelites by setting out God’s standards for holy living. Because of their sinful nature, the Israelites will need to be taught these standards and have disputes resolved using values derived from these divinely revealed regulations.
**me.** Moses apparently sent Zipporah and his family back to Jethro sometime after the incident of 4:24–26.

This formula could indicate either the beginning of Jethro’s faith (2 Kin. 5:15) or its strengthening (1 Kin. 17:24). In any event, Jeth­ro offers sacrifices and shares the communion meal as a worshipper of the Lord of Israel, the one true God. By delivering the Israelites from Egypt, God has made Himself known to Jethro (cf. 7:5 and note).
“Statutes” perhaps suggests standing regulations, and “laws” suggests instructions or teachings.

Delegation is often difficult for an able leader. Men are chosen here on moral rather than intellectual grounds to deal with simple matters. Difficult cases, perhaps those without precedent, are brought to Moses. This is how Israel’s legal system will later function. No difference is made between the sacred and the secular. The entire law was God’s gift to Israel, and obedience to it amounted to obedience to God.

The Lord liberates His people from Egypt to bring them to Himself, to make them His special possession among all peoples. In order to enjoy this blessing, however, they must obey Him and keep His covenant. The revelation at Sinai manifests the holy character of the covenant God and defines the character and behavior appropriate for God’s covenant people.

The Sinai covenant also underscores the special role of the mediator. The Lord declares His intention to descend and speak directly so that the people might hear and trust Moses forever (19:9). However, the face-to-face revelation so terrifies the people that they plead with Moses to go up to God and receive the commands, then return and report to them (20:18–21).

Another crucial lesson of the theophany and revelation at Sinai is the importance of recognizing the holiness of God.

**19:1 came into ... Sinai.** The wilderness of Sinai probably lay in the southeast region of the Sinai peninsula. Mount Sinai is traditionally identified as Jebel Musa, a mountain with a broad plain at its base that seems to fit the biblical evidence (v. 2; cf. Deut. 9:21 note). Arriving at Sinai possibly seventy days after the Passover, Israel will remain there for almost eleven months (Num. 10:11).

God’s words begin (v. 3) and end (v. 6) with an instruction of God to Moses. What lies in between is a summary of God’s covenant faithfulness and Israel’s covenant responsibilities. God invites the Israelites to enter into this special covenant relationship. He does not compel them by force to accept His lordship over them.

God’s deliverance from slavery was not just liberation, but also adoption. He has brought the Israelites out and carried them through the wilderness to bring them to Himself, to make them His (Gen. 17:7 note).

verse_quote: obey my voice and keep my covenant.
note:
Terms summarizing the proper human response to God’s gracious covenant (Gen. 17:2 note).

**treasured possession.** As the following clause shows, God means that Israel will be His personal treasure within what is more generally owned (1 Chr. 29:3). Israel is separated by God’s election from the world, which belongs in its entirety to Him.

verse_quote: kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
note: Israel is to be a priestly royalty, that is, they are to have the status of both priests and kings. This is the status that Adam and Eve forfeited when they betrayed God in the garden of Eden. The Israelites will be a holy nation because God, the Holy One, will come to dwell among them. The emphasis here falls on Israel’s relation to God rather than on any priestly ministry to the nations, yet Israel’s relation to the Lord also bears witness to the world. What this passage prescribes for Israel, the new covenant makes a reality for believers (1 Pet. 2:9–10; Rev. 1:6; 5:10; 20:6).

verse_quote: be ready for the third day.
note:
Arrangements to ensure ritual purity (washing clothes, v. 10; abstention from sexual intercourse, v. 15; Lev. 15:18; 1 Sam. 21:4) and to safeguard the holiness of the mountain (vv. 12, 13) are commanded in preparation for the theophany, a special visual manifestation of divine presence.

**come down on Mount Sinai.** The mountain is the Lord’s place of meeting with His people, not His residence. The tabernacle is soon to be His earthly dwelling place.

verse_quote: On the morning of the third day.
note:
God comes as promised on the morning of the third day. No natural explanation of vv. 16–19a (e.g., a volcanic eruption) is sufficient. This is a divine manifestation by storm and fire.

**a very loud trumpet blast.** Later, special occasions of worship are signaled by the blast of the horn (Num. 10:10).
This may refer to those who discharged the duties of priesthood prior to the establishment of the Levitical priesthood.

The Ten Commandments, or “Ten Words” of the covenant. These are expressions of the eternal moral values of God that transcend the OT and the NT. The first four commandments describe how the people are to relate to God, while the remainder describe how God’s people are to relate to each other (Deut. 4:13 note). See “The Threefold Use of the Law” at Deut. 13:10.

**20:1** See theological note “The Law of God.”

**God spoke all these words.** God speaks only these commandments directly to the people (vv. 18–20 and notes; 19:9; Deut. 4:10–14; 5:22–27; 9:10; Neh. 9:13). What are called “words” here are elsewhere called “commandments” (34:28; Deut. 4:13; 10:4). The Hebrew for “word” (_dabar_) was the term for stipulations in the political treaties of the time.

The Decalogue (from the Greek term meaning “ten words”) itself possibly reflects the ancient treaty framework (see Introduction: Literary Features). First comes the treaty preamble (“I am the LORD your God,” v. 2), then the historical prologue (“who brought you out of the land of Egypt”). The commandments themselves are the treaty stipulations. God is Israel’s Suzerain-King, to whom the people owe complete allegiance. The absence of penalties indicates that the Decalogue is not a legal code but rather a foundational covenant document. The “ten words” are framed as broad principles and not as legislation intended for use in a law court. These covenant principles are then applied in the “Book of the Covenant,” part of which is a set of sample case laws with penalties attached, which follows (20:22–23:19).
God’s claim comes first. Israel is His by right of creation and redemption. The Lord’s covenant commands are given to those whom He has already redeemed for Himself from enslavement to Egypt (19:4).
Lit. “before My face” or “in My presence.” The Lord is a jealous God who already claims Israel as His (v. 5 note).

The term means something hewn from wood or stone. The prohibited image may be that of the Lord, since other deities have been excluded by v. 2, though the qualifying words “any likeness of anything” suggest that pagan idols may be in view. Israel is to be distinguished from the nations by worship that does not make use of images of God. Images are forbidden, not because there can be none, since God made mankind in His own image (Gen. 1:26, 27), but because God must reveal Himself. He is not subject to human imagination. In His own time, God did provide His own image—Jesus Christ is the true image of the Godhead in bodily form (Col. 1:15; 2:19). See “Syncretism” at Hos. 2:13.

When used of God, this word describes His passion for His holy name, a zeal that demands the exclusive devotion of His people. It is employed when that claim is threatened by other deities (Deut. 6:15; Josh. 24:19).

**third and the fourth generation.** The long­est span of generations represented in a given household at any one time. The severity of God’s judgment on subsequent generations warns those who love their children’s children of the terrible consequences of their sin.
God’s covenant mercy, or steadfast love (Hebrew _hesed_) is His devotion to His people (15:13 note).

God’s name is a gift of grace to Israel. And it is in the name, not through an idol, that Israel has access to God in worship. God’s name is therefore to be revered. This command forbids the use of God’s name in false worship, for incantations or divination, as well as for attesting falsehood or speaking blasphemy (Deut. 28:58). Jesus teaches His disciples to pray that God will hallow His name, and Jesus hallows the Father’s name on the cross (Matt. 6:9; John 12:27, 28).

The Hebrew word (_shabbat_) apparently derives from the verb meaning “to cease”—the Sabbath being the day that regular labor ceased. Exodus cites God’s work of creation as the basis for the command (v. 11), while Deuteronomy bases the Sabbath ordinance on the deliverance from Egypt (Deut. 5:12 and note). The Sabbath ordinance is rooted in both creation and of redemption—it looks backward to God’s good creation (Gen. 2:2, 3) and forward to the final redemptive Sabbath rest for God’s people (Heb. 4:1–11). Just as circumcision is the sign of the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 17), so the Sabbath becomes the sign of the Sinai covenant (31:13), reminding God’s people of their place within God’s purposes for creation and of their salvation from physical bondage in Egypt. Ultimately, the Sabbath points to Christ, our Creator and Redeemer, who brings rest to the people of God (Matt. 11:28; Col. 2:16, 17).

The Sabbath is not designed as a burden, but as a blessed release from hard labor (Mark 2:27). The holiness of the day separates it to the Lord so that it is enjoyed by sharing His rest, celebrating His work of creation and redemption (Deut. 5:15).

With this fifth commandment, the Decalogue turns to human relations, beginning with the family. Honor toward parents anchors society, and it binds children to parents in the community of faith. The promise and implied warning of this commandment are unique in this series. Disrespect for parents is a serious matter, for it also dishonors the Lord.

The Hebrew term used here prohibits more than just murder, hence the KJV translation “Thou shalt not kill.” It refers to the taking of any human life when this is not sanctioned by God, the giver of life. OT legislation distinguishes between manslaughter and premeditated murder, both of which are forbidden but incur different penalties (Num. 35:9–34). The verb here is never applied to Israel at war, and capital punishment was authorized before the revelation of this command (Gen. 9:6; cf. Lev. 24:17; Num. 35:30–34). Human life is sacred because man bears God’s image (Gen. 9:5, 6 and notes).

The commandment emphasizes the importance of faithfulness in human relationships. When such faithfulness is absent from the most intimate of relationships, all relationships are undermined. If Israelites break a marriage covenant, they are very likely to break their covenant with God. See “Marriage” at Mal. 2:16; “Divorce” at Mark 10:2.
Property is placed below life and marriage in God’s scheme of moral values.
See “Oaths, and Vows” at Neh. 5:12.
The awe that recognizes God’s power and glory deters sin (v. 20).
Moses’s authority as God’s mediator is acknowledged. That God actually did speak distinguishes Him from false gods, who cannot speak (vv. 22, 23).

See notes on Lev. 1:3–17 and 3:1. Only two types of sacrifices are briefly mentioned here; the list of sacrifices will be expanded in Lev. 1–7 after the tabernacle is constructed and God comes to dwell among the people.

The reasons for this prohibition are no longer clear. Some suggest that this provision was designed to prevent the Israelites from using the altars of Canaanite holy places, which typically were constructed of cut stones. The altar of burnt offering for the tabernacle was made of wood, covered with bronze. The type of altar described here was used for sacrifices made away from the tabernacle. See note on Deut. 27:5.

The Lord sets forth the obligations of His covenant. Civil and penal case laws are presented at 21:1–22:20; moral imperatives that go beyond what laws might enforce are listed in 22:21–29; instructions for sabbatical periods and the celebration of festivals come in 23:10–19; instructions relating to the occupation of the land of Canaan are given in 23:20–33. The purpose of these covenant obligations was to regulate Israelite life in the Promised Land. Interestingly, many of the laws are paralleled in the Code of Hammurabi.

**21:1 rules.** The Hebrew word here means “precedents,” or guiding principles determined by case decisions. These sample laws, which apply the foundational Decalogue (20:1–17) to society, extend to 22:20.

The case law appropriately commences with laws regulating slavery, for that had been Israel’s position in Egypt. A person could sell himself or his wife into slavery because of poverty or debt (2 Kin. 4:1; Neh. 5:1–5; Amos 2:6). Though the Mosaic law allowed the practice of indentured servitude, abuses were carefully limited (Deut. 15:12 note)—such servitude was limited to six years (v. 2) and the rights of slaves were underscored. See note on 1 Pet. 2:18.

The judges probably held court at God’s sanctuary. Whether the door or doorpost was at the sanctuary or the home is not specified here, but Deut. 15:17 favors the latter. The piercing of the ear was a public indication of permanent slavery.
The sale of a woman as a slave-wife seems intended, hence the protection.

While indentured slavery was accepted in the OT, the clear implications of the Christian gospel led to its abolition (1 Pet. 2:18 note). The laws governing Israel’s life should be interpreted in light of their cultural and social setting. They restrained exploitation and oppression in recognition of man’s “hardness of heart” (cf. Matt. 19:8).

The usual Hebrew word for “child” is used (as in v. 4 and 1:17, 18). The Hebrew verb describes the emergence of a child in Gen. 25:26; 38:28–30. There is no reason to limit the “harm” spoken of to the mother. If there is no lasting harm either to the mother or the child, compensation for the hurt inflicted is to be paid to the husband, fixed by a third party. Otherwise, the penalty is proportionate to the injury to the mother or child. Although the harm to the woman or child was not intentional, there was culpable negligence in disregarding the welfare of the pregnant woman.

The fundamental principle is that punishment should fit the crime (Lev. 24:19, 20; Deut. 19:21). Similar statements are found in the laws of Hammurabi (c. 1750 B.C.). It seems that “eye for eye” was idiomatic for the principle of proportional justice, and that such penalties were not literally imposed as the immediate context clearly shows (cf. vv. 18–21; 26–27).
Harm done by animals is the responsibility of the careless owner, and appropriate compensation must be paid. Since the ox had been involved in blood guilt, its flesh was not to be eaten.

Thieves who compound their guilt by profiting from and disposing the stolen animals are to restore fourfold or fivefold (cf. v. 4). More compensation is required in the case of oxen, which take longer to raise.

The killing of an unknown nighttime burglar does not incur bloodguilt, since confronting the burglar might endanger the homeowner’s life. The daytime thief is readily identifiable, and killing is not justified.

Sorcery, the attempt to determine and influence the future through occult means, is strongly condemned (Deut. 18:9–13; 2 Kin. 21:6; Jer. 27:9–10; Mic. 5:12; Nah. 3:4). The future is in God’s hands alone (Deut. 18:9 note).

This refers to a temporary dweller without family support, much as Israel had been in Egypt.

This text is cited by Paul at Acts 23:5. To question duly appointed authority amounts to questioning God’s authority (Rom. 13:1, 2). Neither God nor the ruler whose authority comes from Him are to be reviled.
Because the firstfruits are symbolic of God’s claim on everything, Israelites are not to hold back this offering (13:2 note).

The substance of 22:21 is repeated, framing the moral obligations set out in 22:21–23:9. These obligations go beyond what courts can enforce and demand exemplary moral behavior.

Like the weekly Sabbath on which it was patterned, the sabbatical year is intended for the good of humanity and of creation (20:8–11 and notes). It reminds Israel that God, the true owner of the land, has entrusted it to them (Lev. 25:2). The land is to lie fallow, and what grew of itself is reserved for the poor, who will not have been able to save sufficient food resources. Leviticus 26:34–35 suggests that the sabbatical year was not always observed, but it is clearly in place at Neh. 10:31.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread occurred in March or April in celebration of the Israelites’ divine rescue from slavery in Egypt. Seven weeks later came the Feast of Weeks, celebrating the harvest of cereal crops such as wheat. Finally, the Feast of Tabernacles celebrated the final harvest and the end of the agricultural season in autumn (September).

Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread are closely associated—the Feast begins the day after Passover. Some have mistakenly argued that the Feast of Unleavened Bread is simply an agricultural festival, but its commemoration of the exodus is clear here. See note on Deut. 16:9–12.

See v. 14; Deut. 16:9–12 and notes. Also known as the Feast of Weeks or Pentecost. The Holy Spirit later came in great power at Pentecost (Acts 2:1–39; cf. Rom. 8:23).

**Feast of Ingathering.** Also called the Feast of Tabernacles or Booths. See v. 14; Deut. 16:13–17 and notes.

**end of the year.** This refers to the end of the agricultural, not calendar, year. See note on 12:2.
The details of this verse apply to the Passover celebration (cf. 12:10).

**You shall not boil.** See note on Deut. 14:21.
