**Red Sea.** See note on 13:18.
Israel is quick to disobey this command (Josh. 9). The collection of covenant obligations ends as it began—with an emphasis upon keeping the first two commandments (20:1–4, 22).

The terms of the covenant having been stipulated, the people ratify the covenant by agreeing to abide by its conditions (vv. 3, 7; cf. 19:8).

**24:1 Then he said to Moses.** Having set out the covenant obligations, God now gives further instructions to Moses and the leaders of Israel. The mention of Aaron and his two sons speaks for the authenticity of the narrative, for the sons were later killed for an offense against God (Lev. 10:1–2).

verse_quote: all the words…and all the rules.
note: This may mark Moses’s delivery of the Book of the Covenant (20:22–23:33), since all Israel has heard the Decalogue (20:1 note). The “rules” are the material in 21:1–22:20.
For another reference to Moses writing, see note on Deut. 31:9.
There is no appointed priesthood as yet. The offerings seal the covenant, indicating that God’s acceptance of Israel is on the basis of blood atonement for sin.
This phrase probably applies to 20:22–23:33, which Moses recorded (v. 4).

The people are sprinkled with “the blood of the covenant,” the blood that puts the covenant into effect (Heb. 9:16–22 and notes). The blood signifies cleansing from sin so that the people might enter the covenant relation, and it underscores that the ultimate penalty for breaking the covenant is death. This ritual, like the Passover, resembles how the Aaronic priests are consecrated for service in the tabernacle. The people are sanctified to become a holy nation (cf. 19:6). Jesus proclaims the fulfillment of the symbolism at the Last Supper when He offers the cup: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26:28).

verse_quote: they saw the God of Israel.
note:
They see a visible manifestation of the Lord, but not the fullness of His glory and power. Moses is later privileged to view the “goodness” and the “back” of God (33:19–23 and notes), though the limited character of the manifestation is emphasized.

**feet.** The description concentrates only on God’s feet, an indication of the partial character of the divine manifestation.

**pavement.** Perhaps the vault of the sky under the throne (cf. Ezek. 1:26).

**sapphire.** The area beneath God’s feet is compared to a pavement of blue lapis lazuli. This semiprecious stone was available in a natural form from Cyprus and Scythia, and in artificial form from Egypt.
His power (4:2 note). Not only do they see God, they eat and drink before Him. Similar meals in celebration of the conclusion of a covenant are recorded at Gen. 31:46; Matt. 26:28.
Moses ascends Mount Sinai to receive the covenant tablets and further instructions regarding Israel’s worship and the tabernacle.
Moses’s absence sets the scene for the golden calf incident in ch. 32.
The term is used for a manifestation of the divine presence. The remainder of Exodus deals with the preparations necessary for God to dwell permanently with His people.

This section goes into great detail regarding the divine pattern for the place where the Lord Himself will dwell among His people. The tabernacle and its ministry are the two central features—details of the tabernacle construction, and the precise elements, manner, and persons to be employed in God’s service are carefully specified. The inauguration of the covenant established God’s kingship over Israel. That kingship is now to be appropriately recognized by the Israelites via the building of a portable residence for God as a symbol of His royal authority over Israel.

**25:1** The materials are to be gathered as freewill offerings from the treasures of the people (12:35, 36). Ironically, while these instructions are being given, the people are contributing gold for an idol at the foot of the mountain (32:1–4).
The nearer the divine presence, the finer and more precious the material required. Metals and colored yarns are listed in descending order of value.

Or violet. Violet and purple dyes were obtained from shellfish; scarlet from insects. These colors were precious because of the cost of the dye. The blue of the tabernacle particularly came to be associated with the Lord (Num. 15:38).

**fine twined linen.** The fine linen was probably Egyptian.

**goats’ hair.** The goat hair was undyed. It was to be used as a first covering for the tabernacle, and over it other skins would be placed (26:14).

The ram skin leather was tanned or dyed, perhaps both.

**goatskins.** The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. Dolphin (text note) and sea cow skin are also possible. Such leather may have been cured only, in which case there may be a descending order of value in the skins selected.

**acacia wood.** A hard, long-lasting wood suitable for carving and overlay.
The stones set in the two shoulder pieces of the ephod were of a substance that could be engraved, such as carnelian, onyx, or lapis lazuli (24:10 note; 28:9–12; 39:6–7).
This term underlines the holy nature of God’s residence. It is holy because the Holy One is present there.

The pattern shown to Moses is a model or plan of the tabernacle to be built (cf. the plan of the temple revealed to David in 1 Chr. 28:19). At the same time, it reflects the heavenly residence which already existed (Heb. 9:24). See Ezek. 43:10, 11.

**tabernacle.** The term means “dwelling place.” With the construction of the tabernacle, God comes to dwell among the Israelites. This marks a radically new stage in the divine-human relationship, because God had no earthly residence prior to this. This tabernacle foreshadows the dwelling of God with humanity in the person of Jesus Christ (John 1:14 note).

The revelation of the pattern for the earthly sanctuary begins with the plans for the ark of the covenant, the most holy object in the tabernacle. This ornate chest later contains the Ten Commandments, the pot of manna, and Aaron’s staff (16:33; 25:16; Num. 17:10; Deut. 10:1–5; Heb. 9:4). The ark is viewed as a footstool of the heavenly throne (vv. 18, 22 and notes).

**cubit.** A cubit is roughly the distance from the tip of the middle finger to the elbow—about eighteen inches.
So that the ark can be moved without being touched (cf. 2 Sam. 6:6, 7). Its holiness and portability are stressed.
The stone tablets of the Sinai covenant. God’s written Word is His witness to the terms of His covenant.

Lit. the “atonement covering,” a place at which estranged parties are reconciled. “Atonement” is the normal English translation for the Hebrew root that means “to wipe away” or perhaps “to cover” the guilt of sin from God’s eyes so that believers may be reconciled with God. Propitiation (i.e., turning away divine wrath and satisfying the claims of divine justice) is effected by blood sacrifice in the OT (Lev. 17:11). This shedding of blood dramatizes the cost of forgiveness, and it points forward to the sacrificial death of Christ on the Cross, where the symbolism of the Passover was fulfilled (1 Cor. 5:7). Paul declares that Jesus has been made the propitiation for our sins (Rom. 3:25; cf. 1 John 2:2).

The “mercy seat” is the ark cover, which is sometimes mentioned in distinction from the ark as the place where God is propitiated. In the Septuagint, the Greek term for “mercy seat” (_hilasterion_) means lit. “place of propitiation” (also in Heb. 9:5).

In the OT, the cherubs are usually associated with the throne of the Lord as guardians or bearers of the throne (1 Sam. 4:4; Is. 37:16). In the pagan world, cherubs were minor deities protective of palaces and temples; here they symbolize angelic guardians (Gen. 3:24). They were perhaps depicted as winged sphinxes (winged lions with human heads).

The Lord is the One “who is enthroned on the cherubim” (1 Sam. 4:4; 2 Sam. 6:2; 2 Kin. 19:15; Ps. 80:1; 99:1; Is. 37:16). The mercy seat becomes the focal point for God’s meeting with His people. The purpose of the exodus was the bridging of the chasm separating God and humanity (29:45, 46).

The revelation of the earthly sanctuary pattern continues with the plans for objects to be housed in the holy place—the table of the bread of the Presence, its dishes, and the golden lampstand. Instructions for the altar of incense, also housed in the Holy Place, are given in 30:1–10.

**25:23 make a table.** Called “table of the bread of the Presence” (Num. 4:7) and the “table of pure gold” (Lev. 24:6, 2 Chr. 13:11) on which the bread was arranged (1 Kin. 7:48). It stood on the north side of the holy place (40:22).

These dishes, all of pure gold, include a plate on which the bread of the Presence was placed, a small pan for the frankincense, a pitcher for the wine libation or drink offering, and a bowl into which this was poured (37:16; Lev. 24:7; Num. 4:7).

This bread can only be eaten by the priests (Lev. 24:8, 9). The careful placement of the twelve loaves (probably symbolizing the twelve tribes of Israel) before the Lord and the eating of the loaves by the people’s religious representatives (the priests) remind Israel of its constant dependence on God’s life-giving presence.

The lampstand, which stood opposite the table in the Holy Place, is constructed of a talent (about seventy-five pounds) of hammered gold and patterned to suggest a growing almond tree. Perhaps symbolic of new life, the almond tree blossomed in late January, before other trees.

The pedestal and main upright represent the trunk of the tree, out of which grew three branches on either side. The six branches probably rose to the height of the central shaft, with seven lamps (the number signifying completeness) resting on the topmost ornaments of the shaft and branches (v. 37).

God reveals the pattern for the tabernacle proper. The tabernacle, God’s holy dwelling in the midst of His sinful people, serves a double function. On the one hand, it protects the people from the dangers of unauthorized intrusion into God’s holy presence—the curtains of the Most Holy Place, of the Holy Place, and even of the courtyard stand between the people and the threat of God’s consuming holy presence. On the other hand, the tabernacle provides a way of approach to the Lord. Worshipers enter the outer court to pray and offer sacrifices; the priests carry the people’s petitions into the holy place; and once a year on the Day of Atonement, the high priest enters the Most Holy Place, the very throne-room of the Almighty, with a blood atonement to meet the Lord at the mercy seat.

Nevertheless, the tabernacle was a provisional symbol of God’s dwelling with humanity, rather than the full reality. It symbolized the heavenly temple of God (Heb. 8:1–6; 9:1–15) and pointed forward to the dwelling of God with humanity in Jesus Christ, God incarnate in human flesh (John 1:14 note). As the author of Hebrews makes clear, the tabernacle and its ministry were insufficient in themselves (Heb. 10:1–4). Rather, they foreshadowed the final and completely sufficient priestly work of Christ (Heb. 10:11–18). The tabernacle was also viewed as a model of the cosmos, anticipating a future time when God’s presence would fill the whole earth. The vision of the New Jerusalem in Rev. 21–22 reveals the fulfillment of this expectation.

**26:1 tabernacle.** The tabernacle itself, which houses the Holy and Most Holy Places, is forty-five feet long, fifteen feet wide, and fifteen feet high. It is covered with ten curtains woven of expensive fabrics adorned with cherubim. Two sets of five curtains, forty-two feet long by six feet wide, each of fine linen, are connected so as to provide a continuous piece measuring forty-two feet by sixty feet. This is then draped over the wooden framework. This inner covering ends one cubit (18 inches) short of the ground on either side (vv. 1–6).

As protection for the inner curtain, two sets of curtains of goats’ hair are to be joined by loops and clasps to make one curtain of forty-five feet from top to bottom and sixty-six feet from end to end.
The outer curtains are two cubits (three feet) longer than the inner ones and barely reach the ground (v. 1 note).
Two further covers of rams’ skins and goatskins, apparently arranged in that sequence, are made to protect the two inner sets.

These provide the framework on which the curtains are draped. They are planks, or more likely open frames, that are set vertically to provide the sides and back of the structure. They are stabilized with cross bars and anchored in silver bases driven into the ground. There are twenty on each side and six at the back (west).
The frames are supported by fifteen cross members overlaid with gold, five for each of the enclosed sides. The entire structure can be dismantled or assembled in a minimum amount of time.

The interior of the tabernacle tent is to be divided by the “veil of the screen” (39:34; 40:21; Num. 4:5) that separates the inner Most Holy Place from the outer Holy Place. This veil is a tapestry that hangs thirty feet from the entrance to the tent, creating an inner cube fifteen feet square where the ark is kept. This is the Most Holy Place, the throne room where the Lord will meet with Israel’s high priest on the Day of Atonement. The Holy Place, a royal antechamber, extends thirty feet from the veil to the tent entrance.

The gate at the east end is covered by a screen supported by acacia pillars set in bronze sockets. The screen is made of the same material as the inner curtains and the veil, but is of embroidery rather than tapestry since it was further from the Most Holy Place.

The altar of burnt offering is made of acacia wood overlaid with bronze. The horns at the four corners are important in the ritual and were smeared with blood at the consecration of priests (29:12), in the sin offering (Lev. 4:25, 30), and on the Day of the Atonement (Lev. 16:18). They give sanctuary to anyone who lays hold of them (1 Kin. 1:50). This altar differs from those made of earth or uncut stones (20:24–25).
Accessories, being outside of the tabernacle proper, are all of bronze.

The grate details and its function are obscure. It is placed halfway down the altar running from below the ledge of the altar to the ground. Perhaps it is for ventilation of the altar fire. The “ledge” of v. 5 is apparently for priests to stand on when offering sacrifice.
The court is a rectangle of 150 by 75 feet (46 by 23 m) enclosed by white linen hangings seven and one-half feet high that separate it from the surrounding camp of Israel (v. 18).

A thirty-foot opening on the east side was covered by a screen (v. 16). Fifty-six pillars (twenty on the north and south sides, ten on the west, and three on either side of the entrance on the east) in bronze sockets hold up the linen hangings. Another four pillars support the screen. Their arrangement is not specified, and neither is the placement of the tabernacle within the courtyard. The pillars may be held in place by pegs and guy ropes (35:18).

The court apparently consists of two equal seventy-five-foot squares containing the tabernacle proper and the open space before it. The ark and the altar of burnt offering are the respective central objects. The eastern, open half of the court provides public space for sacrifices and the gathering of worshipers.

verse_quote: pure beaten olive oil for the light.
note: Pure olive oil provides a virtually smoke-free light. The lamp is the golden lampstand that stands on the south side of the Holy Place (Lev. 24:1–4).

The tabernacle is so named because God and Israel’s priestly representatives meet there as determined by liturgical regulation. It is not identical with the tabernacle of meeting outside the camp where God meets Moses (33:7 note; Num. 12:4).

Having revealed the pattern of the earthly sanctuary (25:1–27:21), God now reveals the regulations for the priestly ministry of the sanctuary.

**28:1 serve me as priests.** First and foremost, the priests are to serve as mediators between God and humanity. As priests and representatives of a holy God, Aaron and his sons participate in the holiness of the tabernacle and are held to strict standards of ritual purity (Lev. 21:1–22:16). In addition to their ceremonial duties, such as offering sacrifices and caring for the place of worship, they act as judges (Deut. 17:8–13), dispense blessings (Num. 6:22–27), give oracles (Num. 27:21), and teach God’s rules and instructions to the people (Deut. 33:10).

**Nadab and Abihu.** These two sons of Aaron are killed for unlawful activity (Lev. 10:1–2). Aaron is succeeded by Eleazar (Deut. 10:6).
The vestments of God’s holy high priest are of paramount importance. They are designed for glory and for beauty, and they are made of the same expensive materials as the tabernacle.

This sleeveless linen garment decorated with colored thread is made from costly materials and reached from the breast down to the hips. It has shoulder straps with two onyx stones engraved with the names of the tribes, and a waistband (39:2–7). The breastpiece that contains the Urim and Thummim is fastened to the ephod (v. 27; 1 Sam. 23:9–10).
This is a single piece of fabric, folded double to form a square pouch with gemstones bearing the names of the twelve tribes on its front (v. 21) and the Urim and Thummim inside (v. 30).
Ropes of twisted gold thread connect the breastpiece to the shoulder straps of the ephod.

verse_quote: names of the sons of Israel.
note: Aaron carries this reminder of the nation he represents when he enters the Holy Place.

Lit. “lights and perfections.” They are used to receive oracles from God (Num. 27:21; Deut. 33:8; 1 Sam. 23:6–13; 28:6; Ezra 2:63). There is no hint of how they function or what they are—perhaps stones of different colors, or two small objects engraved with symbols or letters of the alphabet.
This blue robe with bells is worn under the breastpiece and ephod to identify and protect the priest when he enters an area of special sanctity.

LORD **.** On the turban of Aaron is fastened a plate or diadem. The same object is called a crown (29:6; 39:30; Lev. 8:9) and worn by kings (2 Sam. 1:10; 2 Kin. 11:12; Ps. 89:39). The engraved plate is of pure gold, and it identifies Aaron as set apart to the Lord and as Israel’s representative.

The other priestly garments are only briefly described. The coat seems to have been a long shirt-like garment worn under the robe. These priestly garments are to be worn in God’s presence (v. 43). Ordinary priests wear plain coats, a less ornate sash, and a headdress different from the high priest’s.
The undergarment is worn so as not to violate the command of 20:26. Ritual nakedness, so common in other ancient religions, is forbidden in Israel.
Or “make them holy,” set them apart from their fellow Israelites for God’s service. To serve within the tabernacle, the priests have to be holy.
Three kinds of grain offering are to be presented (cf. Lev. 2:4–10).
Aaron and his sons cannot enter the tabernacle until they have been ceremonially cleansed by washing and sacrifice has been made for them (cf. Heb. 7:26–28).
Aaron and his sons are to be clothed with sacred garments symbolic of their office. Only Aaron is anointed and thereby authorized to act as chief priest.
Lit. “fill the hand.” Possibly a Hebrew idiom for induction into office, but it may refer to how they will receive meat from the sacrifices offered by the Israelites in the future (cf. vv. 27–28).

Priests lay their hands on the bull calf to symbolize personal identification and substitution in this sin offering. Blood is to be smeared on the horns of the altar of burnt offering as it was for laymen, since Aaron and his sons are still unconsecrated (Lev. 4:25, 30). The remainder of the blood is poured at the bottom of the altar as in the sin offering (Lev. 4:7; 9:9). Certain parts are to be burned on the altar (v. 13), but the remainder is to be burned outside the camp as unclean (v. 14).
This ram will be offered as a dedicatory burnt offering (Lev. 1:3–17 note).
The other ram will be offered as a peace offering (Lev. 3:1 note).
The ear, hands, and feet of the priests (extremities as representative parts of the whole) are cleansed from impurities to consecrate for service.
Normally part of the priest’s portion (Lev. 7:32), it is also burned in this sacrifice for the priests.
The ceremonial waving symbolizes their dedication as gifts to God.

Moses, since he is acting as priest, will receive the breast and the thigh of the ram from the consecration of Aaron and his sons as his portion; thereafter, the priests are to receive these (Lev. 7:31–32).

The requirements for the daily priestly offerings are reviewed (vv. 38–46). The author of Hebrews contrasts these daily sacrifices for sin (whose repetition pointed to their insufficiency) with the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ (Heb. 10:11–14).

This passage states the goal of the exodus (and of the book). God “brought them out of the land of Egypt” that He might “dwell among them” (v. 46; cf. 7:5; 18:10–12 and notes). The covenant relationship between God and His people is fundamentally one of communion between God and humanity (Gen. 17:7; Ex. 6:7).

verse_quote: an altar on which to burn incense.
note: The altar is to be placed in front of the veil at the entrance to the Most Holy Place (v. 6). It is lit by the high priest morning and evening. The smoke that then covers the mercy seat protects the high priest from the divine presence (Lev. 16:13).

The half-shekel atonement money that accompanies each census witnesses to Israel’s dependence on the Lord’s mercy. Their lives are forfeit because of sin and must be redeemed. The lesson of the Passover and the redemption of the firstborn is applied to all Israel (13:15; 22:29; Num. 3:40–51).

**ransom.** Lit. “atonement.” The payment serves as an act of individual atonement and is an assertion of God’s rights over Israel.

The priests wash their hands and feet when they approach the altar or enter the tabernacle for ministry. No dimensions are given for the basin, though Solomon’s temple basins are massive (1 Kin. 7:38). Neglecting to wash might cause death—the holy God is not to be approached casually (vv. 20, 21).

The tabernacle is to be constructed according to the divine design by gifted men who are supernaturally enabled by the Holy Spirit to oversee all the tasks required (vv. 3–6, 11). All the work is described to Moses by God and little room is left for creative variation (25:9).
The name is archaic and means “in El’s [God’s] shadow” (cf. 17:10 note).
Bezalel’s assistant. His name means “the father is my tent.”

The Sabbath commandment is reiterated and designated as the covenant sign of the Mosaic covenant (Gen. 9:12 note). To keep God’s Sabbath is to keep the covenant since the Sabbath is a sign of the special relationship between God and Israel. To disregard God’s Sabbath is to disregard God’s purposes for creation through His redemption of Israel.

See note on Deut. 5:22. Some suggest that these were two identical copies. Consistent with ancient Near Eastern suzerainty treaties, one copy belonged to each treaty partner and the copies were housed in the respective sanctuaries of the suzerain and the vassal. The ark was both the focal point of Israel’s sanctuary and the special dwelling place of God. Hence, both copies were placed in the ark.

**finger of God.** See 8:19a and note.

God’s continued mercy shown to the people of Israel in these chapters is striking indeed. Even after His mighty exodus deliverance and miraculous provisions for them in the wilderness, they respond with complaints, recriminations, and the idolatrous worship of the golden calf (16:2, 3; 17:1–3; 32:1–6). We should note, however, that this section displays not only the treachery of Israel and the kindness of their God, but also the central role of Moses the mediator. Because the Lord is pleased with the mediator, He does not cast off the people and start anew to make a great nation out of Moses (32:10–14).

We should not conclude that Israel’s continuing in God’s favor is due solely to the merit of Moses as God’s mediator. Rather, the ground of Moses’s plea for mercy is his concern for God’s glory and his appeal to the gracious covenant promises God had made to the patriarchs (32:11–14). The crisis of Israel’s disloyalty, and the Lord’s threat to destroy them, is resolved in the faithfulness of God revealed through the successful appeal of the man Moses, who knows God and His intent to glorify Himself by keeping His promises.

**32:1 gathered themselves together.** The phrase is ominous (used of the rebellion of Korah at Num. 16:3; 20:2). The problem is not with Moses’s past leadership, but with his absence.

The bull as a symbol of deity was common in the ancient world. Perhaps a symbol of Apis, the Egyptian fertility bull-god, was meant. Aaron himself may be presenting the calf as a symbol of the true God, and he apparently attempts to blunt the apostasy by building an altar and announcing a festival to the Lord (v. 5). Noting that the Hebrew term _elohim_, translated “gods” in vv. 1 and 4, can be rendered as singular or plural, some have argued that the people are worshiping the calf as a symbol of the Lord (if so, they are still guilty of idolatry; 20:4 note). But the shout of the people is reported here using the plural verb (“brought ... out”) with _’elohim._ The singular form is always used with this noun when it refers to the true God; thus, it is more likely that the people are turning to the bull-god to lead them, in gross violation of 20:2 (cf. Acts 7:39–41).
The first, second, third, and probably the seventh commandments are violated in this festival (v. 6 note; 20:2–7, 14).

They rise from their meal to engage in what is probably a fertility cult orgy (the bull-god Apis was the Egyptian god of fertility). That this festival involves sexual immorality is further indicated by the later reference to shameful lack of restraint (v. 25).
In righteous anger against their idolatry, God does not acknowledge the people as His own. Instead, He designates them to Moses as “your people.”

Anticipating the intercession of Moses, God proposes to destroy the stiff-necked apostates and to make a new nation of Moses. If He were to do so, God would be setting aside His promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Gen. 12:2; 26:4; 28:14).

Moses rejects God’s offer of v. 10. Instead, arguing on the basis of the honor of God’s name (v. 12) and appealing to God’s faithfulness to the covenant promises made to the patriarchs (v. 13), Moses pleads that God would continue to acknowledge Israel as His people.
Elsewhere the sequence is “Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (cf. 2:24; 3:6; Deut. 1:8), but the substitution is made by Moses to suit the occasion.

LORD **relented.** See note on Gen. 6:6. Moses’s intercessory prayer itself is also part of God’s will and purpose to show His grace. But the effectiveness of Moses’s intercession can only be described by characterizing the Lord in human terms: He relents and withholds the total judgment He had threatened.

verse_quote: work of God ... writing of God.
note: Attention is emphatically drawn to the divine origin of the tablets to be smashed. See theological note “Special Revelation and the Bible.”

Moses replies in a short graphic poem with a threefold use of the word for “singing,” which lit. reads: “Not the sound of singing victory, not the sound of singing defeat, but the sound of singing I hear.”
The broken tablets of the Ten Commandments powerfully picture the broken covenant (20:1 note).

The calf seems to be wooden with a golden overlay. Israel was forced to drink this symbol of their sin to demonstrate that they would bear the responsibility for it (cf. the water of bitterness that an accused adulteress must drink, Num. 5:18–22).

In Aaron’s pathetic defense he blames the people for his own unfaithfulness, and even suggests a miraculous origin for the calf (v. 24). Aaron’s conduct throughout this episode suggests that the Levitical priesthood is destined for failure from its inception (Heb. 5:2, 3; 9:7). Divine judgment upon Aaron is averted only by Moses’s intercession (Deut. 9:20; 10:6–9 and note on 10:6).

LORD’S **side.** Only the Levites, Moses’s own tribe, answer his call to arms to put down the rebellion. They are prepared to use the sword of judgment against neighbors and even family members (v. 28; cf. Num. 25:1–9).
Lit. “filled the hand.” See note on 29:9.

verse_quote: I will go up to the
note: LORD **.** Although the rebellion has been put down, Israel’s guilt before God still looms. Moses again must leave Israel and climb the mountain to meet the Lord.

verse_quote: blot me out of your book.
note: As there is a register of Israel (cf. Num. 1–4), so God Himself has a register of His people (Ps. 56:8; Is. 4:3; Mal. 3:16). If God will not forgive His people, Moses asks to be disinherited with them (cf. vv. 10, 11). Note the similar attitude of Paul in Rom. 9:3.

Moses’s intercession is partially successful: God does not finally reject His people, but the sinful individuals will be judged. The limitations of Moses’s mediatorial office and ministry point to the need for a greater mediator who will present a full and efficacious atonement for sin (Heb. 3:1–6; 10:11–18). See “Jesus Christ as Mediator” on p. 2157.
Israel’s punishment is presented as certain but undefined. Apparently, a plague was soon added as a temporary punishment (v. 35). According to 1 Cor. 10:8, twenty-three thousand people died.
“You” suggests that God absolves Himself of responsibility for Israel since the covenant has been broken (32:7 note).

verse_quote: I will send an angel before you.
note: This is possibly a different angel than the Angel of the Lord that appeared to Moses in the burning bush (3:2). The key to understanding God’s proposal is found in v. 3 (“I will not go up among you”). At issue is God’s gracious dwelling in the midst of the people (29:44–46). If God does not dwell in Israel’s midst, then there is no point in building the tabernacle; indeed, Israel can “depart” immediately without constructing it (v. 1). Instead, another arrangement, already in operation (described in vv. 7–11), is continued. God will meet with Moses and with inquiring Israelites at a tent “outside the camp, far off from the camp” (v. 7). This new “tent of meeting” is not God’s dwelling; Joshua accompanies Moses there (v. 11). God will come in the pillar of cloud from time to time to the entrance of the tent to speak with Moses (vv. 9, 10).

One might think that the Israelites should rejoice at the prospect of receiving their inheritance in the land without the threat of God’s immediate presence. Instead, they mourn, for no longer will Israel be a nation of priests, enjoying immediate fellowship with God (19:3–6; 29:45, 46). This episode is one of the great crises of the Exodus story.

They strip off the festive dress associated with idolatry (cf. Gen. 35:4) and assume the posture of mourners. But this is remorse, not true repentance. They have been and will continue to be a stiff-necked people. Still, there is a note of hope in God’s words, “that I may know what to do with you.”

The Hebrew verbs used here indicate this was the customary practice during the period at Sinai. This “tent of meeting” was a temporary structure that served as a meeting place for God and Moses until the tabernacle proper could be built (v. 2 note).

**outside ... far off from.** At this stage God is not present among the people in the camp.

LORD **.** Moses responds to the dismaying threat of vv. 1–3. He cannot argue that Israel is not stiff-necked, or that the golden calf is an uncharacteristic aberration. He can only plead God’s grace and covenant mercy. He does so by repeatedly asking for precisely what the Lord threatened to withdraw: the revelation of His own Presence (vv. 13–18). Moses’s faithful persistence in intercession is grounded in God’s covenant promise of divine-human communion (6:7; 19:5, 6; Gen. 17:7 note), and reminds us of Jacob’s persistent struggle with God in the quest for divine blessing (Gen. 32:24–30).

**whom you will send with me.** Moses wants to know who will go with him, for he is not prepared to lead the people without God accompanying them.

**I know you by name.** God eariler declared His knowledge of Moses, implying a personal relationship (32:10; 33:11), and will repeat that assurance expressly (v. 17). Because the Lord knows Moses by name personally and intimately, Moses will know the Lord (Num. 12:6–8).
Moses will know the Lord Himself and His purposes for Israel.

Lit. “face.” God Himself will go with Moses.

**give you rest.** Use of the singular pronoun “you” means that the promise of 3:13–15 for all Israel is now repeated for Moses alone.

Moses prays for God’s presence to go with “us,” linking Israel with himself. If God chooses not to go with His people by dwelling among them, it will be useless to go to the Promised Land. The goal is not just milk and honey in Canaan, but a holy land where God will dwell with His people.
Israel’s distinctness is grounded in the gracious presence of God Himself.
God includes Israel for Moses’s sake; Israel depends upon Moses as mediator. Moses’s intercession is a type of Christ’s work as the new covenant Mediator (cf. Heb. 3; 9:16–22).

The Lord sealed His covenant with Israel by revealing Himself (24:9–11), and Moses now seeks a further revelation of God in His glory. His only hope for God’s continuing mercy to Israel lay in God Himself. Having tasted God’s mercy, Moses yearns for a full disclosure.

Though the visible magnificence of this theophany is apparent from the text, the emphasis falls on a revelation to Moses of God’s sovereign, gracious, and compassionate nature (cf. 34:5–7). In Jesus Christ, the glory of the gracious and compassionate God that was withheld even from Moses is displayed to believers through the Spirit (John 1:14; 2 Cor. 3:18).

**to whom ... on whom.** The Lord is sovereign in His purposes of mercy (Rom. 9:14–16). See “Predestination” at Mal. 1:2.
The Lord’s goodness withholds what Moses cannot bear and reveals all that he can.
The replacement of the tablets signals the renewal of the covenant (20:1 note).
The uniqueness of Moses’s mediatorial office is emphasized. The encounter of ch. 19 is to be repeated, but this time with Moses only (cf. 19:24; 24:9)., 3
LORD **descended.** This is the revelation promised in 33:19–23: Yahweh passed by and proclaimed His name. Moses receives an overwhelming answer to his prayer (33:19 note).

This description of God is foundational for later Israelite knowledge of God (Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jon. 4:2; Nah. 1:3). God’s mercy is still proclaimed toward Israel despite her dismal failure (Hos. 11:8). Remarkably, in the light of the golden calf incident, these verses contain echoes of 20:4–6. While God forgives the Israelites, the original covenant obligations are not abandoned.

**34:6 abounding in steadfast love.** “Steadfast love” here translates the Hebrew term (_hesed_) denoting God’s covenant faithfulness and devotion to His people (15:13 note). Because of God’s love and faithfulness, He will not abandon His people, but dwell among them in His tabernacle.

verse_quote: go in the midst of us.
note: This is what the Lord said He would not do, because the people were too sinful, too “stiff-necked” (33:3, 5). Now Moses cites their sin as the very reason for the Presence of God. In effect, he is asking the compassionate and merciful Lord of grace to dwell in His tabernacle among His people and forgive their sin. Then comes the amazing request: “take us for your inheritance.” Moses does not say “give us our inheritance in the land” (cf. 33:2, 3), but “take us for your special treasure in Your faithful love” (the thought contained in 19:5).

God warns against apostate practices. The selection of cultic laws points to the area where Israel has sinned or is weak. Singular pronouns are used almost totally throughout, for God is making His covenant with Moses and with Israel through him (v. 27).

These cultic objects were sacred trees or poles that stood beside the Baal altars in Canaan and represented the Canaanite goddess of fertility (Asherah; cf. Judg. 6:25). Israel must not be compromised by adopting the pagan practices of peoples in the land.
The theme continues with allusions to the first (vv. 14–16) and second commandments (v. 17). God begins at the point of Israel’s sin and with the Decalogue that was violated.
This section parallels the cultic instructions in the Book of the Covenant (23:14–19).
The commands of vv. 12–26.

verse_quote: he wrote ... the words of the cov­enant.
note: The Lord Himself writes the Ten Commandments on the tablets (v. 1; 20:1 note).

Lit. “sent out horns.” Although the Hebrew root usually refers to horns, it seems that rays of light are in view here (cf. Hab. 3:4). Moses’s leadership is confirmed by the reflected light of God’s glory.

verse_quote: they were afraid to come near him.
note: The reaction of fear recalls the events of chs. 19 and 20. Only when they draw near and converse without harm are they reassured.

verse_quote: put a veil over his face.
note: The purpose of the veil is not to calm the anxiety of the people, for Moses puts on the veil only after the people come near and after he finishes declaring the covenant obligations to the people (vv. 31, 32). Rather, as Paul makes clear, the veil is to keep the Israelites from seeing that the glory is fading away (2 Cor. 3:13). According to Paul, this fading glory shows the temporary and inadequate character of the old Mosaic covenant and points to the need for a greater covenant Mediator—Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 3:12–4:6).
The work on the tabernacle starts with an admonition to keep the Sabbath, just as the instructions for the work had concluded with such a reminder (31:12–18).

This entire section is based on chs. 25–31 but follows a different order. While chs. 25–31 give the instructions for the tabernacle, this section describes its construction. Beginning with the reiteration of instructions for the gathering of offerings and artisans (35:4–19), the narrative then moves logically to the gathering of materials and the recognition of artisans (35:20–36:7), the construction of the tabernacle parts and contents (36:8–38:31), the preparation of sacred vestments (39:1–31), the erection of the tabernacle (39:32–40:33), and finally to the climactic arrival of the glory of the Lord in the tabernacle (40:34–38).

Women are mentioned for the first time. Their involvement both in the donation and preparation of the materials is significant (vv. 25, 26, 29). They, no less than the men, are to worship the Lord from their hearts. Their relationship to the Lord is personal and not subsumed under their husbands’ relationship to God.
The work of Bezalel, Oholiab, and their crew of skilled laborers is recounted. The detail of the account underscores the attention paid by the builders to the word of the Lord (39:42–43).

At the recognized ratio of three thousand shekels to the talent (a talent was roughly 75 pounds [34 kg]), a total of 2,193 pounds (995 kg) of gold, 7,544 (3,422 kg) of silver, and 5,310 (2,409 kg) of copper is collected. The amount of silver, a total of 301,175 shekels, is linked to the head count of the Israelites: half a shekel from all males over the age of twenty (603,550 men of military age; Num. 1:46). See note on 30:12.
The finished components are brought to Moses for inspection. Moses received the instructions from the Lord (chs. 25–31), and only Moses can determine the fitness of what has been made.

The Lord’s detailed instructions to Moses regarding the erection of the tabernacle and the consecration of tabernacle and priests (vv. 1–15), together with the subsequent narrative of Moses’s obedience (vv. 16–33), emphasize that the tabernacle is completed and its ministry inaugurated in precise obedience to the divine commands.
The tabernacle is set up about nine months after the arrival at Sinai.

verse_quote: washed their hands and their feet.
note: Following the placement of the basin, Moses and Aaron comply with the law of priestly washing (30:19–21).

The glory of the Lord filling the tabernacle brings the book of Exodus to a climax. God, who brought Israel out of Egypt, makes and renews His covenant with them and makes His dwelling in their midst. A careful recapitulation of the primary theme of the book—the reestablishment of God’s dwelling with man—is given in vv. 34–38. This passage also indicates that Israel has begun corporate worship. The history of God’s guidance to the Promised Land will follow in the remainder of the Pentateuch.
Israel’s journeys are linked to the guiding Presence. The covenant God dwells among His people at last and will lead the nation to the land He promised them.
